content:
"Northern Territory police had long been warned about the dangers lurking within their caged vehicles, but the warnings went unheeded. For years, reports of self-harm and suicide attempts piled up, each one a grim reminder of the system’s failures. Coroner Greg Cavanagh’s findings were damning: police had ignored a 2013 recommendation to install CCTV in the vans, despite 16 attempted suicides in the intervening years. In six of those cases, the individuals were only discovered when they were barely conscious. 'It wasn’t a matter of if a person would die in the back of a police van but when,' Cavanagh had declared, his words heavy with foreboding.

Then, on a warm September night, fate intervened. Two officers, en route to a noise complaint, stumbled upon a horrific crash—a Toyota Hilux wrapped around a palm tree near Darwin airport. Amid the wreckage, they found Dale Scott Walkinshaw, 23, cradling a young woman he had met at a bar. She was drifting in and out of consciousness, her back injured from the impact. Walkinshaw, though unharmed, reeked of alcohol, his blood alcohol level nearly three times the legal limit.

As the officers moved to arrest him, Walkinshaw’s panic set in. He had seen the inside of those caged vans before—knew the stories, the whispers of those who hadn’t made it out alive. But this time, it was different. This time, the system’s neglect would claim another life. By dawn, Walkinshaw was found lifeless in the back of the van, his death a tragic fulfillment of the coroner’s grim prediction. The officers’ failure to act, the ignored reports, the absence of cameras—all of it had led to this moment. And as the news spread, the question lingered: How many more would have to die before change came?"
